Credo Technology Group vs. Western Digital: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?
Sara Appino, The Motley Fool

The race for faster data processing is pushing infrastructure to its limits, forcing a choice between specialized connectivity and massive storage. You might be deciding between Credo Technology Group (NASDAQ:CRDO) and Western Digital (NASDAQ:WDC) for 2027.

Credo provides high-speed connectivity solutions that enable artificial intelligence data centers to communicate efficiently, while Western Digital is a global leader in both hard disk and flash storage. While they operate in different niches, both are essential players in the scaling of cloud infrastructure. This comparison evaluates which stock offers the best path for long-term growth.

The case for Credo Technology Group

Credo Technology Group specializes in high-speed copper and optical interconnect solutions designed for artificial intelligence infrastructure. The company sells products like Active Electrical Cables and optical components to hyperscale operators and system vendors. It has established key partnerships with Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) and Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) to enhance connectivity for dual-architecture systems.

The demand for faster semiconductor stocks has significantly boosted its financial performance. In the 12 months ended Aug. 1, 2026, revenue reached nearly $1.6 billion, representing a 165.1% increase over the previous period. This expansion led to a net income of roughly $538.3 million and a net margin of about 33.8%.

As of its May 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is 0.0x, meaning the company carries no debt relative to shareholder equity. Its current ratio is approximately 10.2x, indicating a strong ability to cover short-term debts with current assets. In the fiscal year ended May 2, 2026, free cash flow reached nearly $407.0 million, though stock-based compensation represented roughly 39.3% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

The case for Western Digital

Western Digital designs and supplies essential data-storage solutions for enterprises and hyperscale cloud providers. Its product portfolio includes both hard disk drives and flash-based storage serving a global market across Asia and the Americas. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk, with three individual clients accounting for 16%, 15%, and 13% of total net revenue in its latest annual report.

In the 12 months ended Oct. 2, 2026, revenue reached approximately $14.5 billion, representing a 43% increase compared to the prior year. Net income for this period was nearly $10.0 billion, which indicates a net margin of roughly 69.2%. This performance suggests a robust recovery in cloud storage demand, which now accounts for nearly 89% of its net revenue.

Cerebras Systems (NASDAQ:CBRS) continued to rebound from its lows, climbing 11% on Nov. 13 after the stock reported soaring revenue and announced a deal with Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT). However, the semiconductor stock is still down more than 40% from its $185 IPO price in May, and more than 70% off its highs.

Cerebras, which makes systems built around its wafer-scale chips the size of an iPad, has thus far been more of a niche provider of high-end artificial intelligence inference (AI) systems with a small customer base. As such, the deal with Microsoft is important, as Cerebras continues to expand its client list, which now includes OpenAI, Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN), and Oracle (NYSE:ORCL). As the company's systems move into the mainstream, it still looks like a good time to buy the stock.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: The Motley Fool.

Surging revenue

In addition to the big deal with Microsoft, Cerebras also addressed rumors around OpenAI, which is set to become its largest customer. It noted that it didn't have enough capacity to provide the system behind OpenAI's ultra-fast mode for its latest models, and that this was why its solution wasn't used, not for technical reasons.

Cerebras has a take-or-pay contract with OpenAI worth more than $20 billion for 750 megawatts of capacity, accounted for in its remaining performance obligations (RPOs), which total $26.1 billion as of the end of September. Notably, the Oracle and Microsoft deals were signed after the quarter and are not in that amount. Due to delays, Cerebras may owe OpenAI delay credits, which were deducted from its RPOs.

Despite some hiccups with OpenAI, Cerebras saw its revenue jump 55% to $210.8 million. Its core sales figure, which strips out revenue distortions from customer warrants and pass-through accounting, soared 70% to $230.9 million, topping the $214.7 million consensus, as compiled by LSEG.

Customers continue to prefer renting its systems, leading to its cloud revenue climbing 265% year over year to $141.9 million and its core cloud revenue surging 287% to $144.9 million. Hardware revenue sank 29% year over year to $68.9 million, while core hardware revenue slipped 11% to $86 million.

Gross margins have been an issue for Cerebras. Its core gross margins came in at 41%, up 30 basis points versus a year ago. Core gross margin for its cloud operation was 46.9%, a big improvement from 16.5% a year ago. However, its core hardware gross margin was 31%, down from 50.5% a year ago. The company said this was due to the continued ramp of its manufacturing capabilities and the final shipments of hardware to early customers under special pricing. Its long-term target for hardware gross margins is 60%. Meanwhile, its cloud gross margins were impacted by Cerebras renting back some equipment from a customer.

title: Oracle Stock Slides 6%, but Bernstein Says It’s Worth $133 Even if Its AI Data-Center Business Fails
detail:
Oracle Stock Slides 6%, but Bernstein Says It’s Worth $133 Even if Its AI Data-Center Business Fails
Oracle Stock Slides 6%, but Bernstein Says It’s Worth $133 Even if Its AI Data-Center Business Fails
Daragh Thomas

ORCL
Trade Oracle on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Benzinga and Yahoo Finance LLC may earn commission or revenue on some items through the links below.

Oracle Corp. (NYSE:ORCL) fell more than 6% Friday, but Bernstein argues investors are overlooking what would survive a failed AI expansion: its databases, business software and conventional cloud operations.

Bernstein analyst Mark Moerdler estimates those businesses could support a $133 share price even if Oracle's AI data-center revenue disappeared, its hardware became worthless and the company still had to pay the debt incurred to build it.

Oracle traded at $103 Friday morning as chipmakers led another day of selling in AI stocks. That's below the $133 Moerdler thinks it would be worth even after a failed AI expansion.

What Remains After an AI Failure?

Bernstein expects Oracle's databases, business software and conventional cloud services to keep earning money even if its AI data-center business fails. Its calculation values those surviving businesses at roughly 25 times their expected earnings over the next year.

In that scenario, Oracle would still have to pay for data centers its AI customers no longer use, and Moerdler says investors may already assume Oracle cannot find replacement tenants, leaving it "holding the proverbial bag" on about $288 billion in lease commitments.

But he thinks Oracle could find other cloud customers to fill those facilities. The payments also stretch over leases lasting as long as 19 years, spreading the bill rather than making it payable all at once.

That argument depends on demand surviving elsewhere. His $133 estimate does not cover a worldwide collapse in generative AI demand, which could make finding replacement customers much harder.

Shares Fall Below the Offering Price

Oracle priced $10 billion of new shares at $116 on Nov. 2, alongside $10 billion of bonds carrying interest rates of 7% to 8.65%.

Friday's price leaves those shares almost 11% below the offering price.

Traders Price a Broader Downturn

On Polymarket, traders put the chance of an AI industry downturn, as the contract defines it, at approximately 26% by June 30th, 2027, with $198,000 traded.

The contract requires three of six triggers in the same 90-day period, including steep stock-price declines and falling computing rental prices. It measures financial stress across the industry, rather than the complete global AI failure Bernstein excludes.

Moerdler remains bullish, with an Outperform rating, equivalent to a buy, and a $325 price target, more than three times Friday's share price.

Oracle (ORCL) Has a $664B Backlog. Can It Fund It?

Trade Oracle on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

We just published a list of the 10 Potential Multibagger Stocks to Research for Long-Term Growth and Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) ranked 10th on this list.

Reuters reported on November 5 that the Nasdaq Composite fell 5.52% to 24,315, its deepest one-day drop in 19 months, while the S&P 500 lost 4.36% and about $3 trillion in market value disappeared. The trigger was Democratic wins in Congress, including in states where opposition to new data centers has grown. That stoked fears that tougher regulation could slow the AI buildout that helped lift stocks to records this year. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index plunged more than 12% on the day, according to the same report, and for anyone searching for stocks that could double over three to five years, a selloff of that size moves the conversation from momentum to staying power.

Oracle (ORCL) Has a $664B Backlog. Can It Fund It?
Why AI Took the Biggest Hit

Melissa Brown, a global head of investment decision research, told Reuters that investors appear to be recognizing that new lawmakers and governors want to slow AI infrastructure development. She added that the AI growth story has largely depended on building out the supporting infrastructure, so any slowdown raises real concerns. Those concerns fall hardest on companies whose growth is tied to data center spending. Our ranking of AI infrastructure stocks to hold for the long term covers that group in more detail.

The weakness carried into the following week. Reuters reported on November 16 that the Nasdaq tumbled 2.5% and the S&P 500 dropped nearly 2%, as fallout from the resignation of a leading chipmaker's chief executive soured enthusiasm for AI stocks. Rate worries added to the pressure. According to the Associated Press, minutes released on November 18 showed that nearly all Federal Reserve officials expect a 25-basis-point rate increase in December, and two floated a 50-basis-point move.

What Long-Term Investors Weigh

Not everyone read the November 5 selloff as the start of a longer slide. Jed Ellerbroek, a portfolio manager, told Reuters it felt like the capitulation phase for companies that benefit from data center spending. Ipek Ozkardeskaya, a senior analyst, added that investors buying into a major AI public offering may sell existing tech holdings to pay for it. That concern showed up on November 19, when Reuters reported that the Nasdaq turned negative at midday as the AI developer's record-setting debut cast a cloud over AI-linked stocks. That leaves a market weighing policy risk, borrowing costs and AI demand all at once, and our list of undervalued growth stocks looks at the valuation side of that trade-off.

Today's big story: Will 2027 Be A 2022 Repeat For Stocks?

CoreWeave (CRWV) shares closed at $44.91 on November 19, 2026, leaving them 67.5% below their highest close of the past year set in May. The stock dropped even as the company more than doubled its revenue over its last four quarters. CoreWeave still lost money over those quarters, making a purchase now a bet that the growth turns into profit. So would a buyer today be early, paying before CoreWeave has shown that profit?

Sitting through CoreWeave's 67.5% drop since May would test anyone's nerves. When a single holding can swing that far, too much of your savings can end up riding on its next report. Instead of one company, the Trefis High Quality (HQ) Portfolio owns 30 quality companies in equal amounts, and it is up more than 105% since September 2020. Look inside HQ.

CoreWeave Costs Less On Sales, But Earns Less

A buyer today pays a lower price for a business that has not yet shown a profit. CoreWeave trades at 2.5 times its sales over the past twelve months, down from 15.8 times at the end of September 2025. Its gross margin, though, fell to 8.5% over the four quarters to September 30, 2026, from 18.6% a year earlier. That margin counts the wear on its equipment, called depreciation, as a cost. In Q3 FY2026 alone, it was 12.4%, up from 7.3% in Q2 FY2026. Over those four quarters it also posted an operating loss of $76 million.

On the cash its operations bring in, the stock looks cheaper. That cash flow does not subtract depreciation, since wear on equipment uses no cash. It trades at 3.5 times its operating cash flow, against 15.0 times for the S&P 500. Yet CoreWeave spends far more than that cash on new capacity. Its free cash flow over the same twelve months was an outflow of $20.4 billion. Its revenue backlog, the revenue from signed contracts not yet earned, is about $133 billion. Management expects to fund most of the spending still needed to deliver it with loans tied to specific customer contracts.

That borrowing already shows on the balance sheet. CoreWeave's total debt was $66.2 billion at September 30, 2026, equal to 263.8% of its market value at the latest close. A year earlier, total debt was $18.8 billion. For the S&P 500, debt is 20.3% of market value. Interest expense in Q3 FY2026 was $846 million, up from $310 million a year earlier. So a buyer at today's price gets a company with thinner margins and far heavier debt than a year ago.

How Fast Is CoreWeave Expected To Grow?

Analysts expect revenue of about $4.9 billion for Q4 FY2026, against $3.66 billion in Q3 FY2026. That would be a rise in sales of about 35% in a single quarter. Management raised its full-year 2026 revenue guide to $13 billion to $13.3 billion.

A $19 Billion Fund Just Bought These 3 Stocks ©@yhelfman via Canva, @Yurich84 from Getty Images via Canva
Key Takeaways

A fund that manages $19.26 billion made Oracle, Boeing and Micron its three biggest buys of the third quarter, according to its 13F filed Nov. 16.

All three have fallen since Sept. 30. Analysts' average targets are now 126% above Micron's price, 114% above Oracle's and 45% above Boeing's.

The fund also holds put options on all three, each with a bigger notional value than its calls.

Of the three, Micron is the one I'd buy because analysts keep raising its earnings estimates and it trades at about 4x forward earnings.

Oracle (ORCL:NYSE), Boeing (BA:NYSE) and Micron (MU:NASDAQ) are all well below their highs, and one big fund just showed it was buying all three.

They were Pentwater Capital Management's three biggest new or added positions in the third quarter, according to its 13F for the quarter ended Sept. 30, filed Nov. 16. Pentwater manages $19.26 billion in all, and its 13F holds $13.16 billion of US stocks across 53 positions.

It also holds puts on all three, each with a bigger notional value than its calls. A 13F doesn't show short positions, and it doesn't show whether those puts hedge the shares.

Oracle is cheap, but its cash hasn't turned yet

Pentwater held 11.75 million Oracle shares at Sept. 30. They were worth $1.61 billion, or 12.3% of its 13F stocks, making Oracle its second-biggest position. The share count rose nearly 13,000% over the quarter. The fund also held calls with a notional value of $323 million and puts with a notional value of $656 million. Oracle is down 19% since Sept. 30.

The worry is cash. Consensus has free cash flow at negative $34.7 billion in fiscal 2027 and negative $27.0 billion in fiscal 2028. S&P has said OpenAI accounts for about half of Oracle's $664 billion backlog. Even so, fiscal 2028 normalized EPS estimates have edged up to $11.06. At about 13x forward earnings, Oracle trades far below its five-year average of about 21x.

Analysts' average target has come down over the past year, from $347 to $236.

The stock fell much further, from $226 to $111, so that target is now 114% above it.

Boeing's estimates are still heading the wrong way

Pentwater added 39% to its Boeing stake over the quarter, bringing it to 8.61 million shares worth $1.60 billion at Sept. 30. That's 12.2% of its 13F stocks. The fund also held calls with a notional value of $188 million and puts with a notional value of $588 million. Boeing is down 14% since Sept. 30.
